name: Point estimate
seoTitle: Point estimate Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Point estimate: work out number of successes from the z score and the MLE. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Point estimate calculator turns the z score, the MLE and the laplace estimation into number of successes. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Point estimate calculator work?
sections.html:
The Point estimate calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of successes in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the z score, the MLE and the laplace estimation.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Point estimate calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of successes=MLE × number of trials
Number of successes=laplace estimation × number of trials + 2 × laplace estimation − 1
Jeffrey estimation=(number of successes + 1 ÷ 2) ÷ (number of trials + 1)
Number of successes=wilson estimation × number of trials + wilson estimation × (z score ^ 2) − 1 ÷ 2 × (z score ^ 2)
Confidence level=-((1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2) × z score)
Best point estimate=(MLE, laplace estimation, jeffrey estimation, wilson estimation)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Number of trials = 10, Confidence level = 95 % and MLE = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Number of successes = 100, Laplace estimation = 8 and Jeffrey estimation = 9.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of successes = 100, Laplace estimation = 8 and Jeffrey estimation = 9 should be roughly the size you expected from Number of trials = 10 and Confidence level = 95 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Point estimate calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the z score, the MLE and the laplace estimation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Point estimate calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of successes, derived from the z score, the MLE and the laplace estimation. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Point estimate calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the z score, the MLE and the laplace estimation, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter confidence level in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Confidence level opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of successes = 100. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Point estimate calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
